newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOYBEANS - Credit still key to Brazil crop size.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEANS - Credit still key to Brazil crop size.

text.p: Preliminary indications are that Brazil's 1996/97 soybean crop should reach a new record in excess of 26 million tonnes but much still depends on the release of credit to farmers, analysts said.

Independent consultants Safras e Mercado yesterday issued its first full estimate of the 1996/97 crop, plotting it at a potential 26.38 million tonnes up from 23.29 million in 1995/96 and also from the previous record of 25.9 million in 1994/95.

"The estimate is working on the basis of planted area of 11.52 million hectares but this area is not guaranteed, specifically because of the amount of money so far made available to farmers," said Safras analyst Flavio Franca.
Credit problems are one of the key reasons why the Agriculture Ministry's National Supply Company (Conab) is expected to issue a more conservative forecast this week.
An Agriculture Ministry official told Reuters last week that Conab is looking more at around 24.50 million tonnes rather than the 26 million tonnes plus forecast by other bodies.
The Conab forecast is expected to be published on October 31, an Agriculture Ministry spokeswoman said.

Of a 5.2 billion reais ($5.05 billion) promised by the government for Brazil's total 1996/97 harvest, around 1.5 billion ($1.46 billion) is expected to be used for soybeans, said an official at the National Agriculture Confederation (CNA).
So far however Banco do Brasil has only released 1.7 billion reais and private banks a further 400 million, said Antonio Donizeti Beraldo, head of the CNA's economics department.
Of the Banco do Brasil total, some 500 million reais have been contracted for soybeans between July and October 28, said a Banco do Brasil spokesman.
"The funds are not reaching the producer. The Banco do Brasil is proving to be very demanding in its criteria to receive credit, it is being very bureaucratic," he said.
One problem directly affecting soybeans at the moment is a shortage of top quality seeds, availability of which is 30 percent down from last year.

As a result farmers are having to use either soybeans or lower quality seeds, both of which will impact on productivity, Donizeti said. But Safras e Mercado maintains that the 750,000 tonnes of certified seeds reported to be available should be sufficient for 71 percent of planted area, which is the average percentage planted with certified seeds in Brazil.

The international as well as the domestic market will be watching carefully over the coming months for any problems which might affect the size of the crop, said Antonio Bueno, economist at the Sao Paulo Commodities and Futures Exchange (BM&F).
"Global supply in the first half of 1997 will be very much determined by the size of the coming Brazil crop," Bueno said.
"A good Brazilian crop could see prices falling to $6/6.50 per bushel. If there are any problems, on the other hand, prices may rise to $7.50/8 a bushel," he added.
Some analysts have also expressed concern that the recent sharp fall in soybean prices may result in less enthusiasm on the part of farmers to plant soybeans.
However farmers say even at these lower levels, prices are still well above the norm.

"I believe we will see 26 million tonnes because we have a good outlook for prices which are currently 20 to 30 percent above the historical average," said Dilvo Grolli, president of Coopavel Cooperatve in Cascavel, Parana state.
